0. Libraries and data

if (!dir.exists(plots_dir)) {
  dir.create(plots_dir, recursive = TRUE)
}

2. Data cleaning

2.1 - 2.6 Blanks, missing values and duplicates

# 2.1 Create a working copy of the original dataset
books_clean <- books

# 2.2 Convert blank strings or whitespace-only strings to NA safely across character columns
character_cols <- names(books_clean)[sapply(books_clean, is.character)]

for (col in character_cols) {
  books_clean[[col]][!is.na(books_clean[[col]]) & trimws(books_clean[[col]]) == ""] <- NA
}

# 2.3 Check missing values after string-to-NA conversion
print(colSums(is.na(books_clean)))
##       price       pages avg_reviews   n_reviews       star5       star4 
##           2          12         123           0           0           0 
##       star3       star2       star1      weight    language 
##           0           0           0           3           3
# 2.4 Count exact duplicate observations
n_duplicates <- sum(duplicated(books_clean))
cat("Total duplicate rows found:", n_duplicates, "\n")
## Total duplicate rows found: 1
# Display all rows involved in duplicate groups
duplicate_rows <- which(
  duplicated(books_clean) | duplicated(books_clean, fromLast = TRUE)
)
print(books_clean[duplicate_rows, , drop = FALSE])
##     price pages avg_reviews n_reviews star5 star4 star3 star2 star1      weight
## 564 44.99   306           5         2     1     0     0     0     0 1.16 pounds
## 765 44.99   306           5         2     1     0     0     0     0 1.16 pounds
##     language
## 564  English
## 765  English
# 2.5 Remove exact duplicate observations (keeping the first occurrence)
books_clean <- books_clean[!duplicated(books_clean), , drop = FALSE]

# Reset row indices
rownames(books_clean) <- NULL

# 2.6 Verify cleaned dataset dimensions and zero duplicates
cat("Cleaned dataset dimensions:", dim(books_clean), "\n")
## Cleaned dataset dimensions: 945 11
cat("Remaining duplicate rows:", sum(duplicated(books_clean)), "\n")
## Remaining duplicate rows: 0

2.7 - 2.8 Weight conversion to kilograms

# 2.7 Inspect weight column to find the units of measurement
# Extract measurement units from the weight column
weight_units <- gsub("[0-9\\.]", "", books_clean$weight)
weight_units <- trimws(weight_units)

# 2.8 Convert weight to kilograms
# Extract numeric portion of weight string
weight_numeric <- as.numeric(gsub("[^0-9\\.]", "", books_clean$weight))


books_clean$weight_kg <- ifelse(
  weight_units == "ounces",
  weight_numeric * 0.028349523125,
  ifelse(
    weight_units == "pounds",
    weight_numeric * 0.45359237,
    NA_real_
  )
)
#Inspect converted weight results
print(head(books_clean[, c("weight", "weight_kg")]))

## 1 12.5 ounces 0.3543690
## 2 1.28 pounds 0.5805982

# Calculate the first and third quartiles

upper_bound <- Q3 + 1.5 * IQR_weight

# 2.12 Detect outliers in other numeric variables (IQR method)

# Function that returns the number of IQR outliers of a variable
count_outliers <- function(x) {
  q1 <- quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)
  q3 <- quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)
  iqr <- q3 - q1
  sum(x < q1 - 1.5 * iqr | x > q3 + 1.5 * iqr, na.rm = TRUE)
}

# Apply the function to the main numeric variables
outlier_vars <- c("price", "pages", "avg_reviews", "n_reviews", "weight_kg")
print(sapply(books_clean[, outlier_vars], count_outliers))
##       price       pages avg_reviews   n_reviews   weight_kg 
##          97          17          34         111          41
# 2.13 Consistency checks for review variables

star_vars <- c("star5", "star4", "star3", "star2", "star1")

# Books without reviews have undefined star proportions
books_clean[books_clean$n_reviews == 0, star_vars] <- NA

# Check star proportions only for books with reviews
reviewed_books <- books_clean$n_reviews > 0

star_sum <- rowSums(
  books_clean[reviewed_books, star_vars]
)

# Summary of star proportions
print(summary(star_sum))
##    Min. 1st Qu.  Median    Mean 3rd Qu.    Max. 
##    0.99    1.00    1.00    1.00    1.00    1.02
# Count inconsistencies (tolerance: 0.05)
print(sum(abs(star_sum - 1) > 0.05, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 0
# Check average rating range
print(range(books_clean$avg_reviews, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 1 5
# Check invalid price and page values
print(sum(books_clean$price <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 0
print(sum(books_clean$pages <= 0, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 0
# Count books without reviews
print(sum(books_clean$n_reviews == 0))
## [1] 123
# 2.13b Rating consistency check
# Compare the reported average rating with the weighted average
# implied by the star-rating proportions
calculated_rating <- 5 * books_clean$star5 +
                     4 * books_clean$star4 +
                     3 * books_clean$star3 +
                     2 * books_clean$star2 +
                     1 * books_clean$star1

rating_difference <- abs(books_clean$avg_reviews - calculated_rating)

# Books for which both ratings are available
valid_rating <- !is.na(rating_difference)
print(sum(valid_rating))
## [1] 822
# Exploratory threshold: difference greater than 0.2
rating_issue <- valid_rating & rating_difference > 0.2
print(sum(rating_issue))
## [1] 90
print(round(100 * mean(rating_difference[valid_rating] > 0.2), 2))
## [1] 10.95
# Number of books with different levels of discrepancy
print(sum(rating_difference > 0.5, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 41
print(sum(rating_difference > 1.0, na.rm = TRUE))
## [1] 15
# The 10 largest discrepancies
rating_check <- data.frame(
  avg_reviews = books_clean$avg_reviews,
  n_reviews = books_clean$n_reviews,
  calculated_rating = calculated_rating,
  rating_difference = rating_difference
)
print(head(rating_check[order(-rating_check$rating_difference), ], 10))

# 2.16 Estimate typical grams per page

# Calculate grams per page
g_per_page <- books_clean$weight_kg * 1000 / books_clean$pages

# Flag potentially implausible values
suspicious_weight <- !is.na(g_per_page) &
  (g_per_page < 0.3 | g_per_page > 10)

# Use only observations with available, non-suspicious ratios
valid_gpp <- g_per_page[
  !is.na(g_per_page) & !suspicious_weight
]

# Calculate the mean and median
print(mean(valid_gpp))
## [1] 1.835052
print(median(valid_gpp))
## [1] 1.71858
# Check how much the values vary
print(sd(valid_gpp))

)

# 3.1 Select the numeric variables
# Use weight_analysis for the filtered weight summary

num_vars <- c(
  "price", "pages", "avg_reviews", "n_reviews",
  "star5", "star4", "star3", "star2", "star1",
  "weight_analysis"
)


# 3.2 Define a function to calculate skewness
# Positive: right-skewed distribution
# Negative: left-skewed distribution
# Close to zero: approximately symmetric

skewness <- function(x) {
  x <- x[!is.na(x)]

  if (length(x) < 3 || sd(x) == 0) {
    return(NA_real_)
  }

  mean((x - mean(x))^3) / sd(x)^3
}


# 3.3 Define a function for descriptive statistics

describe <- function(x) {
  c(
    n = sum(!is.na(x)),
    missing = sum(is.na(x)),
    mean = mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    median = median(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    sd = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    variance = var(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    min = min(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    Q1 = unname(quantile(x, 0.25, na.rm = TRUE)),
    Q3 = unname(quantile(x, 0.75, na.rm = TRUE)),
    max = max(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    range = diff(range(x, na.rm = TRUE)),
    IQR = IQR(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    CV = sd(x, na.rm = TRUE) / mean(x, na.rm = TRUE),
    skewness = skewness(x)
  )
}

summary_table <- t(
  sapply(books_clean[, num_vars, drop = FALSE], describe)
)

4.8 Variability, log transformations and correlation heatmap

To analyse the variability of the variables, histograms of all numerical variables are constructed. Most variables are right-skewed; the only left-skewed variable is the average rating, which suggests that customers leave positive reviews more often than negative ones. The skewed variables are log-transformed with log(1 + x). The + 1 is needed because n_reviews contains zeros (123 books without reviews). To see how the transformation affects the data, the numerical variables are plotted against the average rating before and after the transformation; the average rating was chosen as a possible response variable. Finally, a correlation heatmap of the main numerical variables is constructed.

# Ensure the plots directory exists
if (!dir.exists("plots")) {
  dir.create("plots", recursive = TRUE)
}

hist(books_clean$pages, main = "Distribution of Pages", xlab = "Pages", col = "lightgreen", border = "black")

hist(books_clean$weight_kg, main = "Distribution of Weight", xlab = "Weight (kg)", col = "grey", border = "black")

dev.off()

books_clean$log_n_reviews <- log(books_clean$n_reviews + 1)
books_clean$log_weight    <- log(books_clean$weight_kg + 1)

# 5. Correlation Matrix & Heatmap
# Select only numeric columns for correlation
numeric_vars <- books_clean[, c("price", "pages", "n_reviews", "avg_reviews", "weight_kg")]

# Calculate the correlation matrix
cor_matrix <- cor(numeric_vars, use = "complete.obs")

# Draw and save the correlation heatmap securely
png("plots/correlation_matrix_basic.png", width = 1200, height = 1200, res = 150)

corrplot(cor_matrix, 
         method = "color",       # Uses color blocks
         type = "upper",         # Shows upper triangle to avoid duplication
         addCoef.col = "black",  # Prints correlation coefficients inside boxes
         number.cex = 0.7,       # Size of text numbers
         tl.col = "black",       # Text label color
         tl.srt = 45,            # Rotates text labels 45 degrees for readability
         main = "Correlation Matrix of Book Variables",
         mar = c(0, 0, 2, 0))

dev.off()
## png 
##   2
# Print the matrix (complete cases only: books with reviews and weight)
print(round(cor_matrix, 2))
##             price pages n_reviews avg_reviews weight_kg
## price        1.00  0.49     -0.07       -0.08      0.34
## pages        0.49  1.00      0.06        0.06      0.57
## n_reviews   -0.07  0.06      1.00        0.07      0.01
## avg_reviews -0.08  0.06      0.07        1.00      0.04
## weight_kg    0.34  0.57      0.01        0.04      1.00
print(sum(complete.cases(numeric_vars)))
## [1] 811

Interpretation. After the log transformation, the points are spread more evenly instead of being concentrated in the lower-left corner. In the heatmap, price and pages have a moderate positive correlation and pages and weight a strong one, which is expected because longer books need more material. The average rating shows correlations close to zero with all the other variables. Note that this heatmap uses only complete cases (books with reviews and a weight), so its price–pages coefficient differs slightly from the one computed on all available pairs.

Correlation matrix heatmap. The heatmap shows the Pearson correlations among all numerical variables (pairwise complete observations).

  • Price and pages: moderate positive correlation (r = 0.44); longer books tend to be more expensive.
  • Average rating and star proportions: strong positive correlation with star5 (r = 0.68) and negative correlations with lower ratings (star3: r = -0.49, star4: r = -0.40). This is mathematically expected, because the average rating is a weighted combination of the star proportions.
  • Multicollinearity: the correlations among the core explanatory variables (pages, price, n_reviews) are low.

Pairwise scatter plot matrix. The plots involving n_reviews and price show strong right skewness, with most observations at low values, which supports the use of log(1 + x) transformations. The plots involving star1–star5 show bounded, constrained patterns because the proportions of each reviewed book sum to one. The matrix also includes the log-transformed variables and both weight variables created earlier.

# 2. Price before and after the log(1 + price) transformation
png("plots/price_vs_log_price_histograms.png",
    width = 12, height = 5, units = "in", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(1, 2))

hist(books_clean$price, main = "Distribution of Price",
     xlab = "Price", col = "lightblue", breaks = 30)
hist(log(1 + books_clean$price), main = "Distribution of log(1 + Price)",
     xlab = "log(1 + Price)", col = "lightgreen", breaks = 30)

par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
dev.off()
## png 
##   2

Distribution of book prices. Price is clearly right-skewed with a long right tail. Most books are priced roughly between 30 and 50, while a small number of specialised or academic titles reach 200 and beyond. This skewness justifies the log(1 + price) transformation, which reduces the influence of the most expensive books and makes the distribution more symmetric for the subsequent tests and regression.

Distribution of average ratings. avg_reviews is left-skewed and bimodal. The main peak is around 4.5, and a second peak appears at exactly 5.0. The second peak is likely driven by books with only a few (exclusively positive) reviews; as the number of reviews grows, ratings tend to move towards about 4.5. Books with low average ratings (1.0–3.0) are rare.

Distribution of pages. Page count is right-skewed. Most books have roughly 300–400 pages, while a smaller group of comprehensive works exceeds 1,000 pages. This asymmetry should be kept in mind when modelling price, since effects in the long tail are estimated from few books.

Distribution of star rating proportions.

  • star5 is left-skewed, concentrated mainly between 0.60 and 0.85, with a spike at 1.0: some books have exclusively five-star reviews, typically books with few reviews.
  • star4 is moderately right-skewed, mainly between 0.10 and 0.25, with a spike at 0.
  • star3, star2 and star1 are strongly right-skewed and concentrated at 0; the spike at zero becomes larger as the star level decreases.

Customer ratings are therefore predominantly positive. Because the five proportions sum to one for every reviewed book, they are perfectly collinear and cannot all enter the same regression model; at least one category must be left out.

5. Hypothesis testing

Hypothesis 1: Price vs page count

  • H0: no correlation between pages and log(1 + price).
  • H1: page count is significantly correlated with log price.
# --- Hypothesis 1: Price vs Page Count (OLS vs. LOESS vs. Nadaraya-Watson) ---

# 1. Perform Pearson correlation test to evaluate linear association
cor_test_h1 <- cor.test(books_clean$pages, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "pearson")
print(cor_test_h1)
## 
##  Pearson's product-moment correlation
## 
## data:  books_clean$pages and log(1 + books_clean$price)
## t = 16.944, df = 929, p-value < 2.2e-16
## alternative hypothesis: true correlation is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.4352112 0.5334718
## sample estimates:
##       cor 
## 0.4858752
# Keep only books with both pages and price, so the (x, y) pairs stay matched
cc_h1 <- complete.cases(books_clean$pages, books_clean$price)
nw_fit <- as.data.frame(
  ksmooth(books_clean$pages[cc_h1],
          log1p(books_clean$price[cc_h1]),
          kernel = "normal", bandwidth = 100)
)

# 2. Visualize the models using ggplot2 (handling missing values on-the-fly)
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = pages, y = log(1 + price))) +
  # Scatterplot representing individual book observations
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#2c3e50") +
  
  # Linear OLS regression fit (parametric baseline)
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", aes(color = "OLS Linear"), se = FALSE, linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  
  # LOESS (Local Polynomial Regression) fit to capture non-linearities
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", aes(color = "LOESS (Local Poly)"), se = FALSE, linewidth = 1) +
  
  # Nadaraya-Watson Kernel Regression estimator (local constant smoothing)
  geom_line(
    data = nw_fit,
    aes(x = x, y = y, color = "Nadaraya-Watson"),
    linewidth = 1
  ) +
  
  # Define custom colors for each estimation method
  scale_color_manual(
    name = "Estimation Method",
    values = c("OLS Linear" = "red", "LOESS (Local Poly)" = "blue", "Nadaraya-Watson" = "darkgreen")
  ) +
  
  # Add titles, axis labels, and statistical context
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 1: Price vs. Page Count",
    subtitle = "Comparison of Parametric (OLS) and Non-Parametric (LOESS & Nadaraya-Watson) Estimators",
    x = "Page Count (pages)",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_1_price_pages.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

Result. Pearson’s test gives a significant positive correlation between pages and log price (r = 0.486, t = 16.94, df = 929, p < 2.2e-16, 95% CI 0.435–0.534), so H0 is rejected.

  • Up to about 800 pages, where most books lie, the OLS line, the LOESS curve and the Nadaraya–Watson estimator closely agree.
  • Above about 1,000 pages the data are sparse. The Nadaraya–Watson estimator is a local average, so there it follows individual books, producing sharp fluctuations and flat segments.
  • The LOESS curve is smoother, but its downward bend is also based on very few books; the OLS line extrapolates into a region with almost no data.

Page count is positively associated with log price where most books lie; estimates for books above 1,000 pages are unreliable.

Hypothesis 2: Price by review status

  • H0: mean log price is the same for books with and without reviews.
  • H1: the means differ.
# --- Hypothesis 2: Price Differentiation by Review Engagement ---

# 1. Create a binary engagement variable based on review counts
books_clean$has_reviews <- factor(
  ifelse(!is.na(books_clean$n_reviews) & books_clean$n_reviews > 0, "With Reviews", "No Reviews")
)

# 2. Perform Welch Two-Sample t-test
t_test_h2 <- t.test(log(1 + price) ~ has_reviews, data = books_clean)
print(t_test_h2)
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  log(1 + price) by has_reviews
## t = 2.7354, df = 151.67, p-value = 0.006973
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group No Reviews and group With Reviews is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.04619552 0.28647661
## sample estimates:
##   mean in group No Reviews mean in group With Reviews 
##                   3.943061                   3.776725
# 3. Visualize the price distribution across review status (Boxplot & Violin plot)
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = has_reviews, y = log(1 + price), fill = has_reviews)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("No Reviews" = "#e74c3c", "With Reviews" = "#2ecc71")) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 2: Price Comparison by Review Status",
    subtitle = "Welch Two-Sample t-Test on Log-Transformed Prices",
    x = "Review Engagement Status",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# 4. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_2_price_reviews.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

Result. Welch’s t-test shows a significant difference in mean log price (t = 2.74, df = 151.67, p = 0.007, 95% CI 0.046–0.286), so H0 is rejected at α = 0.01. Books without reviews have a higher mean log price (3.943) than books with reviews (3.777). The “With Reviews” group also shows more extreme high-price values. One possible explanation is that newly listed, unreviewed titles are offered at their full list price, while popular titles are discounted over time; the data do not allow this explanation to be tested directly.

Hypothesis 3: Ratings by review engagement

  • H0: average rating is the same for high- and low-engagement books (split at the median review count).
  • H1: average ratings differ between the two groups.
# Hypothesis 3: Ratings Variation Across Review Engagement Levels 
# Note: Since avg_reviews is structurally NA for books with zero reviews, 
# we evaluate rating variation within the subset of reviewed books based on review volume (median split).

# 1. Filter for books with reviews and valid average ratings
reviewed_books <- subset(books_clean, !is.na(avg_reviews) & n_reviews > 0)

# 2. Create binary engagement groups (High vs. Low based on median review count)
median_reviews <- median(reviewed_books$n_reviews, na.rm = TRUE)
reviewed_books$engagement_group <- factor(
  ifelse(reviewed_books$n_reviews >= median_reviews, "High Engagement", "Low Engagement")
)

# 3. Parametric Two-Sample Welch t-test
t_test_h3_alt <- t.test(avg_reviews ~ engagement_group, data = reviewed_books)
print(t_test_h3_alt)
## 
##  Welch Two Sample t-test
## 
## data:  avg_reviews by engagement_group
## t = 2.008, df = 534.01, p-value = 0.04515
## alternative hypothesis: true difference in means between group High Engagement and group Low Engagement is not equal to 0
## 95 percent confidence interval:
##  0.001231847 0.112276609
## sample estimates:
## mean in group High Engagement  mean in group Low Engagement 
##                      4.469378                      4.412624
# 4. Non-parametric Wilcoxon rank-sum test (Mann-Whitney U)
wilcox_h3_alt <- wilcox.test(avg_reviews ~ engagement_group, data = reviewed_books)
print(wilcox_h3_alt)
## 
##  Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction
## 
## data:  avg_reviews by engagement_group
## W = 83962, p-value = 0.8886
## alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0
# 5. Boxplot & Violin plot Visualization
p <- ggplot(reviewed_books, aes(x = engagement_group, y = avg_reviews, fill = engagement_group)) +
  geom_violin(alpha = 0.3, trim = FALSE) +
  geom_boxplot(width = 0.2, outlier.color = "red", alpha = 0.7) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("Low Engagement" = "#3498db", "High Engagement" = "#9b59b6")) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 3: Average Ratings by Review Engagement Level",
    subtitle = "Comparing High vs. Low Review Count Subsamples (Welch t-test & Wilcoxon)",
    x = "Engagement Group (Based on Median Review Count)",
    y = "Average Rating (avg_reviews)"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(legend.position = "none")

# 6. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_3_ratings_engagement.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

Result. Within the 822 reviewed books, Welch’s t-test finds a small significant difference (t = 2.01, df = 534.01, p = 0.045): the High Engagement group has a slightly higher mean rating (4.469 vs 4.413). The Wilcoxon rank-sum test, which does not assume normality and is less sensitive to the strong left skewness and low-rating outliers, is not significant (W = 83962, p = 0.889). The evidence that review volume is associated with different ratings is therefore not robust. These results should also be read in light of the rating consistency check (Step 2.13b).

Hypothesis 4: Review volume vs price

  • H0: n_reviews is not correlated with log price.
  • H1: the two are correlated.
# --- Hypothesis 4: Review Volume (n_reviews) vs Log Price ---
# 1. Spearman Rank Correlation (robust against heavy tails)
cor_h4 <- cor.test(books_clean$n_reviews, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
print(cor_h4)
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  books_clean$n_reviews and log(1 + books_clean$price)
## S = 161572930, p-value = 1.465e-06
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##       rho 
## -0.156073
# 2. Scatterplot with Log-Log Scale and LOESS fit
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = log(1 + n_reviews), y = log(1 + price))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#2980b9") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "darkblue", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 4: Log Review Volume vs. Log Price",
    subtitle = "Spearman Correlation & Non-Parametric Fit",
    x = "Log Review Count (log(1 + n_reviews))",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_4_reviews_price.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

Result. Spearman’s test shows a weak negative correlation (rho = -0.156, S = 161572930, p = 1.5e-6), so H0 is rejected. Books with more reviews tend to be cheaper.

Hypothesis 5: Average rating vs price (quality premium)

  • H0: avg_reviews is not correlated with log price.
  • H1: the two are correlated.
# 1. Spearman Rank Correlation
cor_h5 <- cor.test(books_clean$avg_reviews, log(1 + books_clean$price), method = "spearman", exact = FALSE)
print(cor_h5)
## 
##  Spearman's rank correlation rho
## 
## data:  books_clean$avg_reviews and log(1 + books_clean$price)
## S = 90080069, p-value = 0.5723
## alternative hypothesis: true rho is not equal to 0
## sample estimates:
##        rho 
## 0.01974504
# 2. Scatterplot with LOESS fit
p <- ggplot(books_clean, aes(x = avg_reviews, y = log(1 + price))) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.3, color = "#27ae60") +
  geom_smooth(method = "lm", color = "red", linetype = "dashed", se = FALSE) +
  geom_smooth(method = "loess", color = "darkgreen", se = FALSE) +
  labs(
    title = "Hypothesis 5: Average Rating vs. Log Price",
    subtitle = "Testing the Quality Premium Hypothesis",
    x = "Average Rating (avg_reviews)",
    y = "Log Price (log(1 + price))"
  ) +
  theme_minimal()

# 3. Save the plot using ggsave
file_path <- file.path(plots_dir, "hypothesis_5_rating_price.png")

ggsave(
  filename = file_path,
  plot = p,
  width = 10,
  height = 7,
  units = "in",
  dpi = 150
)

Result. Spearman’s test gives rho = 0.020 (p = 0.572), so H0 is not rejected. In the plot, the OLS line is almost horizontal and the LOESS curve stays flat between 3.5 and 5.0 stars, where most books lie; its movement below 3.0 stars is based on very few books. Higher ratings are not associated with higher prices, so there is no evidence of a quality premium.

6. Multivariate regression

6.1 OLS model for log price

# --- Step 1: Multivariate OLS Model Construction ---
# Model specification based on validated hypotheses (H1, H2, H4)
ols_model <- lm(log(1 + price) ~ pages + has_reviews + log(1 + n_reviews), data = books_clean)

# Summary of the model output
summary_ols <- summary(ols_model)
print(summary_ols)
## 
## Call:
## lm(formula = log(1 + price) ~ pages + has_reviews + log(1 + n_reviews), 
##     data = books_clean)
## 
## Residuals:
##     Min      1Q  Median      3Q     Max 
## -1.8652 -0.2896  0.0159  0.2567  1.9500 
## 
## Coefficients:
##                           Estimate Std. Error t value Pr(>|t|)    
## (Intercept)              3.388e+00  5.260e-02  64.410  < 2e-16 ***
## pages                    1.506e-03  7.935e-05  18.984  < 2e-16 ***
## has_reviewsWith Reviews  4.104e-03  6.065e-02   0.068    0.946    
## log(1 + n_reviews)      -7.220e-02  1.066e-02  -6.774 2.23e-11 ***
## ---
## Signif. codes:  0 '***' 0.001 '**' 0.01 '*' 0.05 '.' 0.1 ' ' 1
## 
## Residual standard error: 0.4831 on 927 degrees of freedom
##   (14 observations deleted due to missingness)
## Multiple R-squared:  0.2924, Adjusted R-squared:  0.2901 
## F-statistic: 127.7 on 3 and 927 DF,  p-value: < 2.2e-16
# --- Step 2: Diagnostic Checks ---

# 1. Multicollinearity check (VIF < 5 indicates no severe multicollinearity)


vif_values <- vif(ols_model)
print("--- Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ---")
## [1] "--- Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ---"
print(vif_values)
##              pages        has_reviews log(1 + n_reviews) 
##           1.046146           1.647483           1.701567
# 2. Diagnostic Plots (Residuals vs Fitted, Q-Q Plot, Scale-Location, Residuals vs Leverage)

file_path_diag <- file.path(plots_dir, "ols_model_diagnostics.png")

png(filename = file_path_diag, width = 10, height = 8, units = "in", res = 150)
par(mfrow = c(2, 2))
plot(ols_model)
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
dev.off()
## png 
##   2

Interpretation. The model is significant overall (F(3, 927) = 127.7, p < 2.2e-16). R² = 0.292 and adjusted R² = 0.290, so about 29% of the variation in log price is explained.

  • Pages (β = 0.001506, t = 18.98, p < 2e-16): holding the other variables constant, each extra page is associated with about 0.15% higher price.
  • has_reviews (β = 0.0041, t = 0.07, p = 0.946): not significant once log(1 + n_reviews) is in the model.
  • log(1 + n_reviews) (β = -0.0722, t = -6.77, p = 2.2e-11): a 1% increase in review count is associated with about 0.072% lower price.

All VIF values are below 2 (1.05, 1.65, 1.70), so multicollinearity is not a problem.

About 71% of the variation remains unexplained. This is typical for cross-sectional pricing data, where price also depends on factors not in the dataset (publisher, binding type, author reputation, discounts).

Diagnostic plots. The residuals are centred around zero with mild curvature (Residuals vs Fitted). They follow the normal line in the centre but deviate in the tails (Q-Q). The spread increases at higher fitted values (Scale-Location), suggesting heteroskedasticity. Some observations have relatively high leverage (Residuals vs Leverage). The OLS assumptions are therefore not fully satisfied, and the results should be interpreted with caution.

6.2 Models for average rating

model_formulas <- list(
  "1. Without Stars" = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews),
  "2. With Star5"    = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews) + star5,
  "3. With Star5 & Star4" = avg_reviews ~ pages + log(1 + price) + log(1 + n_reviews) + star5 + log(1 + star4)
)

# Loop through each specification to fit the model and check diagnostics
for (model_name in names(model_formulas)) {
  
  # Print separator and current model name
  cat("==================================================\n")
  cat("Model Specification:", model_name, "\n")
  cat("==================================================\n")
  
  # Fit the OLS regression model
  current_model <- lm(model_formulas[[model_name]], data = books_clean)
  
  # Print the regression summary output
  print(summary(current_model))
  
  # Calculate and print Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) for multicollinearity check
  cat("\n--- Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) ---\n")
  print(car::vif(current_model))
  
  cat("\n\n")
}

Nested models for the average rating.

  • Model 1 (pages, price, n_reviews): not significant (F(3, 807) = 2.046, p = 0.106, adjusted R² = 0.004). Book characteristics explain almost none of the variation in ratings.
  • Model 2 (+ star5): adjusted R² rises to 0.480.
  • Model 3 (+ star5 and log(1 + star4)): adjusted R² rises to 0.521, with all VIF values below 2.5.

Adding star3, star2 and star1 is not possible without severe multicollinearity, because the proportions sum to one. Important caveat: the average rating is essentially a weighted average of the star proportions, so the high R² of Models 2 and 3 is largely mechanical and does not show that star proportions “explain” ratings in a substantive sense. The main finding is Model 1: book characteristics are not associated with ratings.

6.3 VIF chart

# 1. Calculate VIF values from your fitted OLS model
vif_vals <- vif(ols_model)

# 2. Convert the VIF vector into a clean data frame for ggplot
vif_df <- data.frame(
  Variable = names(vif_vals),
  VIF = as.numeric(vif_vals)
)

# 3. Create the VIF bar chart using ggplot2
p_vif <- ggplot(vif_df, aes(x = reorder(Variable, VIF), y = VIF, fill = VIF)) +
  geom_col(width = 0.6, alpha = 0.8, color = "black") +
  # Add a horizontal dashed line representing the critical threshold (e.g., 5.0)
  geom_hline(yintercept = 5.0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed", linewidth = 1) +
  coord_flip() + # Makes it a horizontal bar chart for clean label reading
  labs(
    title = "Variance Inflation Factor (VIF) Diagnostics",
    subtitle = "Checking for Multicollinearity (Threshold = 5.0)",
    x = "Predictor Variables",
    y = "VIF Value"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(
    legend.position = "none",
    plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 14)
  )

# 4. Save the plot to your specified directory
file_path_vif <- file.path(plots_dir, "vif_diagnostics_chart.png")
ggsave(filename = file_path_vif, plot = p_vif, width = 8, height = 5, units = "in", dpi = 150)

7. Conclusions

  • Page count is the strongest predictor of price. It is positively associated with log price in the correlation test, in both non-parametric fits and in the regression (about +0.15% per page).
  • Books with more reviews tend to be cheaper. This holds in the Spearman test and in the regression. One possible explanation is that popular, mass-market titles are discounted more; the data cannot confirm this.
  • Higher ratings do not come with higher prices. There is no evidence of a quality premium (p = 0.57), and book characteristics explain almost none of the variation in ratings.
  • Data quality. One duplicate was removed, 10 implausible weights were excluded from the weight analysis, and 90 books show a discrepancy between the reported average rating and the star proportions; these were kept and documented.
  • Language was dropped. Almost all books are in English, so the variable provides no useful variation.
  • Limitations. The regression explains about 29% of price variation, and the diagnostic plots indicate non-normal residuals and heteroskedasticity, so the estimates should be interpreted with caution.
